identification.summary: Larva-24005 is AhnLab ASEC's name for a sub-group of Kimsuky, which ASEC describes as receiving North Korean support [S1]. ASEC reported it using compromised servers as phishing infrastructure against people involved with North Korea and university professors researching the regime, with phishing aimed at South Korea and Japan [S1]. In a later ASEC profile, the cluster was tied to intrusions into South Korean software, energy and financial organizations, using BlueKeep (CVE-2019-0708) in some cases, MySpy, RDPWrap and KimaLogger or RandomQuery keyloggers [S2][S3][S4].
identification.firstObserved: Activity since at least October 2023 per ASEC-based reporting [S3][S4]; one advisory says September 2023 [S6].
identification.notes: ASEC treats Larva-24005 as a sub-group of Kimsuky [S1]. Kimsuky is tracked by other vendors under different names; this record does not merge those facts with ASEC's cluster. Strobes states no exploited CVEs are attributed to the actor, which conflicts with ASEC's BlueKeep reporting [S2]; ASEC is treated as authoritative.

attribution.sponsor: North Korea (DPRK), as assessed by AhnLab ASEC, which calls Larva-24005 a Kimsuky sub-group that receives North Korean support [S1].
attribution.confidence: Not stated in the sources reviewed. This is a vendor (AhnLab ASEC) assessment; no government attribution to Larva-24005 specifically was found.
attribution.basis: ASEC's linkage of the cluster to Kimsuky [S1][S3][S4]. The underlying technical evidence for the linkage was not available because the ASEC pages could not be opened (see gaps).

objectives: Collection of credentials and information from individuals involved with North Korea and academics researching the regime, via phishing [S1]. Persistent remote access and keystroke capture on compromised hosts in South Korean software, energy and financial organizations [S3][S4].

regions: A threat advisory lists additional countries, including the US, Canada, Germany, UK, China, Singapore and others [S5][S6]
targeting.notes: Reporting differs on Japan: headlines say attacks on South Korea and Japan, but ASEC's profile describes breached South Korean firms with phishing sent to South Korea and Japan, so Japan appears to be a phishing target rather than a confirmed set of breached victims [S4]. The wider country list comes from a secondary advisory and may reflect victim or phishing recipients [S5].

capabilities.summary: Breaches servers in Korea, sets up a web server and PHP environment there, and uses them for phishing; pages were stored under the IIS_USER account and XAMPP home folder, with traces later deleted [S1]. Phishing emails posed as Zoom meeting links or web portal login pages [S1]. Initial access included BlueKeep (CVE-2019-0708) in some systems, although an RDP scanner found on one system showed no evidence of use, and phishing exploiting Equation Editor CVE-2017-11882 was another route [S3][S4]. Post-compromise, a dropper installed MySpy (system information collection) and RDPWrap to keep RDP access, followed by KimaLogger or RandomQuery keyloggers [S3][S4].

campaigns.name: Start of observed intrusion activity
campaigns.summary: ASEC-based reporting says the campaign against South Korean software, energy and financial firms has been active since at least October 2023; a Hivepro advisory says September 2023 [S3][S4][S6].

campaigns.name: Phishing emails targeting Japan (ASEC report)
campaigns.summary: ASEC reported Larva-24005 used compromised Korean servers as phishing infrastructure and attack base against North Korea-related individuals and professors, and also against Japan, with Zoom-link and portal-login lures and BlueKeep, RDPWrap and a custom keylogger used on infrastructure [S1].

campaigns.name: ASEC APT group profile
campaigns.summary: ASEC published a longer Larva-24005 profile covering intrusions at South Korean software, energy and financial companies and tooling (MySpy, RDPWrap, KimaLogger, RandomQuery) [S2][S4].

campaigns.name: Secondary press coverage
campaigns.summary: The Hacker News and Security Affairs reported ASEC's findings, attributing the cluster to Kimsuky; ThaiCERT followed on 2025-04-23 [S3][S4][S5].

diamond.adversary: Larva-24005, an AhnLab-named Kimsuky sub-group, assessed by ASEC as North Korea-supported [S1].
diamond.capability: BlueKeep exploitation, CVE-2017-11882 phishing, MySpy, RDPWrap, KimaLogger and RandomQuery keyloggers, and PHP/web phishing kits [S1][S3][S4].
diamond.infrastructure: Compromised servers in Korea running IIS/XAMPP with PHP used to host phishing pages and as a C2 base [S1].
diamond.victim: North Korea-focused individuals and academics, South Korean software, energy and financial organizations, and Japanese phishing recipients [S1][S3][S4].
diamond.socioPolitical: Collection on North Korea policy and research communities, consistent with ASEC's Kimsuky linkage [S1].
diamond.technology: Internet-exposed unpatched Windows RDP (BlueKeep), Microsoft Office Equation Editor, IIS/XAMPP web servers, email [S1][S3][S4].

gaps: ASEC primary reports (asec.ahnlab.com/en/86535 and /87554) could not be opened (host unreachable); details rely on search-result summaries and secondary coverage.
Exact first-observed date conflicts (September vs October 2023) [S6][S3].
Attribution confidence and technical basis for the Kimsuky linkage are not stated in accessible sources.
Whether Japanese and other-country entities were breached or only phishing recipients is unclear [S4][S5].
No MITRE group ID, Microsoft name or government attribution identified.
Indicators (hashes, domains, IPs) were not retrieved.

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. Step 1-2: the environment of interest is Korean and Japanese academic, policy and enterprise networks plus exposed Windows RDP and IIS/XAMPP servers [S1][S3]. Step 3 (adversary): a Kimsuky sub-group using compromised third-party servers for phishing [S1]. MLCOA: continued Zoom or portal-login phishing against North Korea experts, hosted on newly compromised servers, with keyloggers and RDPWrap for persistence [S1][S3]. MDCOA: broader victim set across the countries listed in secondary advisories [S5]. Candidate indicators: new RDPWrap installs, IIS_USER or XAMPP web roots holding phishing pages, KimaLogger or RandomQuery artifacts, BlueKeep probing [S1][S3].
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. Situational awareness: share phishing and tooling indicators from ASEC with allied and academic partners once primary indicators are retrieved [S1]. Authorities: activity concerns civilian and allied networks, so response would run through host-nation or owner channels rather than DoD authorities. Mission assurance: ensure legacy Windows RDP hosts are patched against CVE-2019-0708 and Office against CVE-2017-11882 [S3][S4]. Coordination: AhnLab and Korean/Japanese CERTs hold the primary data [S1][S5].
